slides.title: Teaching LLMs Expert Judgment: A Chess RL Case Study
slides.subtitle: Ibrahim El-Fayoumi · Perth Machine Learning Group · Microsoft, 100 St Georges Terrace, Perth
slides.notes: [0:00-1:30] Welcome. One sentence up front: expert judgment is tacit, so it has to be trained into a model, not prompted into it. Tonight: chess with Qwen3-1.7B as the controlled testbed, then the Bridgewater result that shows the same recipe works at production scale.

slides.title: The hook: prompting can't transfer judgment
bullets: Frontier LLMs, six routine investor tasks, prompt that just states the task: ~50% accuracy
Experts rewrite the prompts, automatic prompt optimisation on top: mid-70s - still below the 80% trust threshold
"An explicit prompt can only convey the intuition an expert is able to put into words"
The judgments that matter most are the hardest to articulate

bullets.text: Source: Thinking Machines Lab x Bridgewater AIA Labs, 'Learning to Replicate Expert Judgment in Financial Tasks', 30 Jun 2026

slides.notes: [1:30-4:00] Start with the strongest evidence, not ours. Frontier models averaged ~50% (Opus 4.6: 47.2, Gemini 3.1 Pro: 50.1, GPT 5.4: 47.2...). Expert prompts lifted to mid-70s (77.2, 74.3, 75.8, 78.2, 78.0) - coin flip to C+ student. Prompt optimisation hit a wall. Quote is from the TML/Bridgewater post.

slides.title: The thesis
slides.notes: [4:00-4:30] Transition.

slides.title: Thesis: tacit judgment is trained in, not prompted
bullets: Expert judgment is tacit - it lives in thousands of small decisions, not in a written rubric
Fine-tuning on expert signal lets the model develop its own judgment
A small model trained on expert signal can beat a much larger frontier model
We need a testbed where 'expert judgment' is objective, cheap, and measurable

bullets.text: That testbed is chess: Qwen3-1.7B trained against Stockfish

slides.notes: [4:30-6:30] Chess gives us a perfect expert (Stockfish ~3200 Elo), an exact reward, and infinite labelled positions. Financial judgment at Bridgewater is the noisy real-world version of the same problem. Everything we learn about reward design and credit assignment transfers.

slides.title: Setup: chess as the controlled testbed
slides.notes: [6:30-7:00] Transition to setup.

slides.title: Setup: Qwen3-1.7B + Stockfish reward
bullets: Policy: Qwen3-1.7B - small enough to train on modest compute, large enough to produce legal play
Teacher/reward: Stockfish 17 - an expert ~1000+ Elo above anything the policy can reach
Pipeline: SFT on game transcripts -> GRPO with engine reward -> off-policy extension (LUFFY)
Evaluated on held-out positions (n=1000) + full games vs Stockfish and vs random
slides.notes: [7:00-9:00] Deliberately the smallest credible model. Question we're really asking: how small can a model be and still reason? Three training stages mirror the talk structure.

slides.title: How we measure
bullets: Legal-move rate: can the model play the game at all? (formats, state tracking)
Median centipawn loss (CPL): quality of each move vs Stockfish's best

bullets.text: Use the MEDIAN, not the mean - the mean is dominated by rare blunders (std ~2900 cp)

bullets: Game outcomes vs Stockfish (20 games) and vs random (10 games); avg game length
Estimated Elo
slides.notes: [9:00-10:30] Explain CPL briefly: 0 = engine's move, 100 cp = roughly a pawn of lost value. Legal-move rate is the floor: an LLM that emits 'e4 e5 Nf3' as one token or hallucinates squares fails here. Our headline floor stat: 100% legal moves on 1000 held-out positions.

slides.title: Stage 1 - SFT on game transcripts
slides.notes: [10:30-11:00] Transition.

slides.title: Stage 1 - SFT: what the model learns
bullets: Data: game transcripts (FEN state -> move in SAN), generated with Stockfish
Learns: move format, board syntax, opening patterns, 'what a reasonable move looks like'
Does NOT learn: why a move is good - no signal beyond imitation
Result: 100% legal-move rate on the test set - the model can play
But: median CPL 81 cp, loses 0-20 vs Stockfish (20/20), 0 wins vs random (9 draws, 1 loss)
slides.notes: [11:00-13:00] SFT buys competence, not judgment. The odd result to flag honestly: 9/10 draws vs random. Likely draw-adjudication / move-limit artifacts - we show the numbers as they are. Data format note: transcripts teach the token patterns of chess; the model still has no internal critic.

slides.title: Stage 2 - GRPO with Stockfish as the reward
slides.notes: [13:00-13:30] Transition.

slides.title: Stage 2 - GRPO: reward from the engine
bullets: GRPO: critic-free policy gradient - sample G moves per state, reward each, normalise within the group
Reward: Stockfish evaluation of the chosen move (centipawn signal), plus game outcome
Advantage is relative: 'better than the group's average move', not 'objectively good'
No value network to train - fits our compute budget
Reward shaping: legality penalty, engine eval, game result
slides.notes: [13:30-15:30] Keep GRPO math light here (the notebook does the step-by-step). Key intuition: within a group of sampled moves, the model learns which of ITS OWN candidate moves the engine prefers. That is expert signal, per decision.

slides.title: Failure modes: sparse reward, brutal credit assignment
bullets: One terminal reward spread over ~30 decisions per game - credit assignment is the core difficulty
Long-horizon strategy: a good move's value may only appear 20 plies later
Strategy has no token signature - nothing in the trace says 'this was the strategic move'
Reward hacking pressure: engine-eval shaping can be gamed locally (shallow tactics)
Off-policy drift: by the time a game finishes, the policy that played it is stale
slides.notes: [15:30-18:00] This is the honest heart of the talk. Compare: a chat model gets per-token feedback; our policy gets one scalar after ~30 decisions. That is why RL from game outcomes alone stalls - and it motivates both per-move engine shaping and the distillation stage.

slides.title: Strategic vs tactical: why chess is hard for a 1.7B model
bullets: Tactics (forks, pins): local, 2-4 plies, pattern-shaped - SFT handles these
Strategy (piece activity, pawn structure, plans): global, 20+ plies, no local pattern
Branching: ~35 legal moves/ply - the horizon problem explodes combinatorially
A frontier model 'knows' chess commentary; a 1.7B must learn search-free evaluation
Humans also can't articulate strategic judgment - exactly the tacit-knowledge problem
slides.notes: [18:00-20:00] Tie back to the thesis: strategic judgment in chess is tacit even for humans - club players can't write down why a move 'feels' right. That's the same structure as Bridgewater investors filtering documents.

slides.title: GRPO results - the honest read

bullets.text: Sources: evaluation_results/comparison.json (canonical, frozen 2026-10-19); benchmark_results.json is a stale duplicate rl/final run (29.9 plies, median CPL 102.5) and is not quoted

slides.notes: [20:00-22:30] Numbers are real, from the repo. Say it straight: RL did NOT move the headline evals - median CPL slightly up (81->90), still 0-20 vs Stockfish. What changed: longer games (24.3 -> 27.7 plies) - the policy survives longer, plays differently. Note: benchmark_results.json is a stale duplicate rl/final run - canonical file frozen as comparison.json (2026-10-19); no discrepancy discussion needed.

slides.title: So did RL teach anything new?
bullets: Headline evals flat - but behaviour changed: longer games, different move distributions
RL sharpened and stabilised SFT behaviour rather than adding new capability (so far)
Consistent with the literature: RL mostly reweights what SFT already knows
The gap is signal density, not model capacity - one reward over ~30 decisions

bullets.text: Which sets up stage 3: denser signal from the same compute

slides.notes: [22:30-24:30] This is the 'RL: new capabilities or sharpened SFT?' key question answered for OUR case: sharpening. Bridge to LUFFY/on-policy distillation: the problem isn't the model, it's the reward density.

slides.title: Stage 3 - off-policy learning: LUFFY and distillation
slides.notes: [24:30-25:00] Transition.

slides.title: LUFFY: off-policy guidance from a stronger teacher
bullets: LUFFY: mix a strong teacher's traces into GRPO rollouts, with policy-aware down-weighting
Learns from the expert even where the policy's own samples are all bad
Regularisation keeps the mixture on-policy (importance-based advantage adjustment)
Extra learning from limited compute - we don't need more engines, we need better use of the one we have
slides.notes: [25:00-27:00] Be explicit about repo status: our LUFFY eval is not yet run - the comparison-table cell is empty (audit 2026-10-18). Present LUFFY as the designed next stage, with the TML/Bridgewater ablation as external evidence the recipe class works.

slides.title: Why on-policy distillation helps
bullets: Exposure bias: off-policy training never fixes the states the policy actually reaches
Dense per-token signal vs one terminal reward - credit assignment becomes trivial
The student's own rollouts stay on-policy; only the TARGET comes from the teacher
Cheaper than sampling from a frontier teacher at every state
slides.notes: [27:00-29:00] The key mental model: RL asks 'which of my moves was good?' (sparse, noisy). Distillation asks 'match the teacher's distribution HERE' (dense, per-token, on the states I actually visit). Examples: SFT model sees only Stockfish games, not its own blunders; OPD trains on the model's own states with teacher targets.

slides.title: Evidence at scale: Thinking Machines x Bridgewater
slides.notes: [29:00-29:30] Transition to the payoff.

slides.title: The same recipe, at production scale
bullets: Bridgewater AIA Labs + Thinking Machines Lab, published 30 Jun 2026
Task: six document-triage tasks from real investor workflows (relevancy, labelling, truncation)
Base: Qwen3-235B fine-tuned on Tinker - GRPO start, then interleaved batching + CISPO + on-policy distillation
Expert labels only where needed: contested examples routed to investors for re-review
Result: fine-tuned open model beats every frontier model tested - at 13.8x lower inference cost per task
slides.notes: [29:30-31:30] This is our thesis proven outside chess. Walk the pipeline: contractor labels failed (models trained on them performed poorly) - the fix was routing contested examples to real investors. Note the overlap with our recipe: GRPO + on-policy distillation, same component names.

slides.title: Bridgewater numbers

charts.title: Average accuracy on six financial triage tasks

bullets.text: 84.7% vs 78.2% = 29.8% fewer errors; 13.8x lower inference cost per task. Source: TML/Bridgewater post, 30 Jun 2026 (thinkingmachines.ai)

slides.notes: [31:30-33:00] Read the bars: 44.8 base -> 73.5 after GRPO alone (the biggest single jump, same as our SFT->RL story) -> 84.7 after the full recipe. Their ablations: removing interleaved batching drops to 72.2%; removing OPD drops to 72.4%; CISPO+asymmetric clips 74.6%. A 13.8x cost cut with better accuracy is the production argument.

slides.title: Caveats (say them before the audience does)
bullets: Company-run internal evaluation - not an independent public benchmark
Six tasks, private test set cleared for release; generalisation beyond them unproven
Cost figure covers inference only - expert labelling and training cost not included
Frontier models not improving fast on this axis: GPT 5.4 cost 43% more than 5.2 for marginal accuracy gain
Same discipline applies to OUR numbers: small n, one seed, self-reported
slides.notes: [33:00-34:30] Credibility slide. Both the Bridgewater result and our chess numbers are self-reported on internal evals. State limits, then move to takeaways. This honesty is itself part of the talk's argument about expert judgment.

slides.title: Key questions this testbed answers

bullets.text: How small can a model be and still reason?
1.7B reaches 100% legal play and club-level tactics after SFT; strategic play needs better signal, not more parameters
Does RL teach new capabilities or sharpen SFT?
In our run: sharpening (longer games, stable behaviour), evals flat - consistent with TML/Bridgewater where the recipe, not scale, moved the number
Reward from an engine ~1000 Elo stronger - what goes wrong?
Reward signal too sparse in game outcome; per-move engine shaping helps but invites local (tactical) reward hacking; the stronger the teacher, the more its best moves are unreachable-by-imitation

slides.notes: [34:30-37:00] The three questions from the abstract, answered with our data plus the external evidence. Keep each to ~45 seconds.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Expert judgment is tacit - prompting plateaus (~50-78%), fine-tuning on expert signal crosses the trust threshold (84.7%)
Chess is a clean rehearsal space: real reward design, real credit-assignment pain, honest metrics
Small models + expert signal beat large models + prompts, at a fraction of the cost
On-policy distillation turns a sparse terminal reward into dense per-token learning
The bottleneck is signal quality, not model size
